title: Working at Height — Ladders, EWPs and Roofs
verdict:
No. I would not sign this version and send a crew out on it — but it is close, and the previous round's findings have been genuinely answered rather than gestured at.

WHAT I VERIFIED, SO NOBODY RE-LITIGATES IT. I pulled the consolidated text of the Work Health and Safety Regulation 2011 (Qld), the Work Health and Safety Act 2011 (Qld), the Electrical Safety Act 2002 (Qld) and the Electrical Safety Regulation 2026 (Qld) from legislation.qld.gov.au and read every provision this statement relies on. All six s 291 quotes in hrcw are verbatim. Sections 54, 55(3)(a), 78, 79(3) with its combination note, 80(2)–(4), 213, 289(2)(e) and 289(3)(d), 299(4), 300(2), 316, 317(1)–(2), 425(5)–(6), 427, schedule 3 item 21 and the schedule 19 "scaffolding work" >4m definition all say what the document says they say. The whole 306 series checks out — 306A's definition list is now exactly right and the free fall / limited free fall correction to s 306I(14) is correct (more than 600mm but not more than 2m; not more than 600mm). The anchor citation is not just fixed, it is better than the fix asked for: steps[0].controls[3] now cites s 306I(1) and s 306I(10)(b) and warns the technician in terms not to quote s 306I(10)(c) at an anchorage point, which is the trap the last version walked into. Step 5 is re-rated extreme→high with a real hold point and an engineering control that finally names the case where the machine has no secondary guarding. Step 6's ladder-rail system is now correctly levelled ppe and moved last. The s 306M(7) prohibition is administrative. The exclusion-zone item is split into a real isolate control and an administrative one, and every schedule 2 figure quoted matches the untrained-person table in the 2026 regulation — 3,000mm on foot to 132kV, 4,500 / 5,000 / 6,000 above that, and 3,000 / 6,000 / 8,000 for operating plant. ESR 2026 s 33, s 34, s 36, s 292(1) and (7) and s 296(2)–(4) are quoted accurately, including "enter … includes placing any part of a person's body in the roof space". ES Act ss 11, 12, 18 and 55 are correct. The electric shock and heat paragraphs the last reviewer demanded are there, and they are good — the line-contact paragraph in particular is the best writing in the document. I also cleared the standards caveat the last reviewer could not: AS 2118.1:2017 Amd 3:2024 (February 2024), AS 2550.10:2025, AS/NZS 1418.10:2025, AS/NZS 1891.4:2025 (supersedes 2009), AS 5532:2025 (supersedes AS/NZS 5532:2013), AS 1670.1:2024 (supersedes 2018) and the three 2021 Queensland codes of practice all confirm. No repealed instrument is cited bare — both mentions of the 2013 electrical regulation name the 2026 replacement beside them.

WHAT STOPS IT. Four things, and none of them are in the parts that were corrected — they are in the parts nobody looked at.

First, the solar fix is half a fix. Solar PV was originally named in steps[1].hazards[3] as an obstacle for driving an EWP round a yard or carpark. The correction added strong solar controls to the two roof steps and left step 1 exactly as it was. So the one step that actually deals with putting a machine up in a carpark still names arrays as a hazard and gives the crew nothing for them — and worse, the two electrical controls it does give are both keyed to "overhead electric line", which is the wrong instrument: schedule 2's DC table starts at ±25kV and does not reach a 600–1000V DC string on a carport canopy. The crew gets a rule that does not apply and no rule that does.

Second, this is a working-at-height statement whose emergency field has no response for a fall that is not arrested. There is a paragraph for a person hanging in a harness, one for shock, one for line contact, one for heat, one for a dropped object, one for a crush, one for a stuck machine. There is nothing for the single most likely serious event in the document — a technician off a platform ladder onto a plant room floor. The only paragraph headed with the word "fall" tells the reader to lay the person flat, which is right for suspension and wrong for a spinal injury.

Third, the document contradicts itself on the one thing it is most emphatic about. Three separate places forbid entering or leaving an elevated basket and forbid using an EWP to get onto a roof, and the stuck-machine paragraph goes so far as to say the prohibition "does not become safe in an emergency". Then the heat paragraph tells the crew to bring a collapsed technician off a roof "in the EWP basket". That is one control instructing what another prohibits, at the exact moment a frightened second person is deciding what to do alone.

Fourth, two things the document promotes are under-specified in ways that kill people. It pushes the mobile scaffold twice as the preferred substitute for a ladder and then gives a six-item rule list with no stabilisers and no access rule — the two ways people die on mobile scaffolds. And the rescue step names "rescuer becoming the second casualty" as a hazard, never says the rescuer stays attached on a roof, and allocates the emergency to three people in a statement that crews every roof and harness job for two.

Fix the step 1 solar hole, add a ground-impact fall paragraph, take the EWP basket out of the roof retrieval sentence, put stabilisers and internal access into the scaffold rules, and rewrite the rescue allocation for the crew you actually send — and I would sign this.

blocking.field: steps[1].hazards[3] and steps[1].controls ("Sign in and walk the area before anything goes up")
blocking.problem: A hazard the document names and never controls. steps[1].hazards[3] reads "Overhead electric lines, solar arrays and unfused mains across the yard or carpark". Step 1 has seven controls. controls[0] is the supply-authority isolation of "an overhead electric line"; controls[2] is the schedule 2 exclusion-zone item, also for "an overhead electric line". Neither reaches a solar array, and nothing else in the step mentions one. The correction added genuinely good PV controls to steps[6].controls[7] and steps[7].controls[6] — but those are roof-work controls, and the technician who is putting a boom up under a carpark PV canopy or beside a wall-mounted array reads steps 1, 4 and 5, not 6 and 7. The exclusion-zone control is worse than silent, it is misdirecting: schedule 2's DC table in the Electrical Safety Regulation 2026 (Qld) starts at a nominal pole-to-earth voltage of +/- 25kV, so a 600–1000V DC string on a carport canopy has no prescribed exclusion zone at all, and the crew is left applying a figure that was never written for it. Step 7 states the principle correctly and the statement contradicts itself by omission: "nothing the site can switch off kills the DC side" is true in the carpark too, and step 1 never says so.
blocking.fix: Add an administrative control to steps[1] immediately after the exclusion-zone item, and name PV in steps[1].hazards[3]'s own terms: carport and awning solar canopies, wall-mounted arrays and their DC conduit, cable tray and combiner boxes are live whenever there is daylight, no site isolation and no supply authority isolation kills them, and schedule 2 exclusion zones do not cover them because that table starts at +/- 25kV DC. Rule: do not position, slew or elevate a machine where the basket, the boom, a test pole or a load can reach a panel, rail, conduit, tray, combiner box or DC cable; if the device cannot be reached with that clearance, stop and ring the supervisor for a licensed electrical worker and a route, the same answer steps[6] and steps[7] already give. Add a matching siteSpecificPrompt asking whether the drive path or the work position sits under or beside a PV canopy or array.

blocking.problem: No emergency response for an unarrested fall. The emergency field carries paragraphs for a person hanging in a harness, electric shock, plant in contact with an overhead line, heat illness, a person struck by a dropped object, a person crushed between the basket and structure, an EWP stuck elevated, and fire while the system is impaired. It has nothing for a technician who falls and hits the floor, the roof deck or the ground — which is the event this entire statement exists to prevent and the most likely serious injury in it (a fall off a platform ladder onto a concrete plant room floor, a fall through a ceiling, a fall from a tank ladder). The only paragraph a stressed reader will find under the word FALL is "FALL ARRESTED, PERSON HANGING", and its instruction is "LAY THEM FLAT as soon as it is safe" — correct for suspension, and the wrong first move for someone who has just landed on their back. The right instruction does exist in the document, but it is buried under the dropped-object heading ("Do not move them if they are unresponsive or complaining of neck or back pain"), where nobody will look for it.
blocking.fix: Add a FALL TO THE GROUND — NOT ARRESTED paragraph, placed before the suspension paragraph so the reader hits it first. It needs to say: stop all work above immediately and clear the area below. Do not move them and do not sit them up — assume a spinal injury on any fall over about a metre, or any fall where they hit their head or are not making sense. Check response and normal breathing; if they are not breathing normally, that overrides everything and CPR starts, moving them only as much as the airway needs. Keep them warm and still, control any bleeding, and do not let them get up and walk it off. Ring 000 and send the second person to the gate. Also make it explicit that LAY THEM FLAT belongs to the suspension paragraph only and is not the instruction here.

blocking.field: emergency (HEAT ILLNESS AND HEAT STROKE paragraph), against steps[5].controls[2], steps[6].controls[3] and emergency (EWP STUCK ELEVATED paragraph)
blocking.problem: One control instructs what three others prohibit. The heat paragraph says: "Get them out first: down off the roof or out of the void by the access route already planned, or bring them down in the EWP basket." Applied to the roof case that authorises exactly the manoeuvre the statement forbids everywhere else. steps[5].controls[2] reads "DO NOT CLIMB INTO OR OUT OF THE BASKET WHILE IT IS ELEVATED. Enter and exit at ground level or on the chassis only. You do not step onto a roof, gantry, plant deck, mezzanine or tank top from the basket", and allows the exception only for a machine designed for transfer at height, under a documented risk assessment, with a fall arrest system anchored to the structure and the transfer point named on the permit. steps[6].controls[3] reads "An EWP is not a means of access onto a roof under this statement." And the emergency field's own EWP STUCK ELEVATED paragraph says "Getting out of an elevated basket is what this statement forbids in normal work and it does not become safe in an emergency." So the document tells the second person, alone, with a mate down and a clock running, that the basket is an option — and the thing it invites is one unqualified person slewing a boom to an unprotected roof edge and hauling an unconscious body over the rail. That is a second fatality, not a rescue.
blocking.fix: Cut the EWP basket from the roof half of that sentence. Write the retrieval by location: out of a ceiling void or down from a basket the person is already standing in, use the basket and the ground controls — that is what steps[11].controls[0] is for and it is consistent. Off a roof, the route out is the compliant access already planned plus the rescue kit that steps[11].controls[1] requires to be on the roof, and if the person cannot be moved down that route the second person rings 000 and QFES and keeps cooling in place rather than improvising a transfer at height. Say in the paragraph that the elevated-basket prohibition in steps[5] and steps[6] is not suspended by a medical emergency, in the same words the EWP STUCK ELEVATED paragraph already uses.

blocking.field: steps[3].controls[1] ("Platform ladder and mobile scaffold work in corridors, plant rooms and ceiling spaces")
blocking.problem: The statement promotes the mobile scaffold twice as the preferred substitute for a ladder — steps[0].controls[1] ("For a run of devices down a corridor or a plant room, book a mobile scaffold") and steps[3].controls[1] — and then gives a rule list that omits the two things mobile scaffolds actually kill people with. The control reads "Rules for it: fully decked; guardrails and toe boards fitted; castors locked before anyone climbs; nobody and nothing on the deck while it is moved; no ladder, drum or box on the deck to gain height; scaffold tag current and filled in." Nothing requires the stabilisers or outriggers to be fitted and deployed to the manufacturer's configuration for the bay height in use, and nothing says how you get onto the deck. Overturn of a stationary bay erected without its stabilisers, and a fall from climbing the outside of the frame instead of the internal ladder through the trapdoor, are the two standard mobile scaffold fatalities, and neither appears anywhere in the document — the word stabiliser does not occur, and the only mention of outriggers is for the EWP at steps[4].controls[0]. The overturn hazard is also missing from steps[3].hazards, which names only "Mobile scaffold moved with a person or tools still on the deck" — the moving case, not the standing one. A crew reading a list headed "Rules for it:" will take it as the complete rule set.
blocking.fix: Add to steps[3].hazards a line for overturn of a mobile scaffold erected without its stabilisers or on an uneven or sloping floor, and for a fall while climbing the outside of the frame. Add to steps[3].controls[1], keeping it at substitute: stabilisers or outriggers fitted and deployed in the manufacturer's configuration for the platform height in use, on a firm level floor, before anyone climbs, and the bay not built taller than the manufacturer's permitted height for the base without them; access to the deck only up the internal ladder and through the trapdoor, with the trapdoor closed once you are on the deck — never up the outside of the frame, never up the guardrails; and the bay checked against the manufacturer's plate and the scaffold tag before use. Keep the existing >4m licensed scaffolding work rule as it stands.

blocking.field: steps[11].hazards[3] and steps[11].controls[6] ("Rescue — agreed before the harness goes on, not after the fall")
blocking.problem: Two related faults in the rescue step. First, steps[11].hazards[3] names "Rescuer becoming the second casualty" and the controls only ever answer it for the machine: steps[11].controls[0] keeps the rescuer on the ground controls of the EWP, and the emergency field answers it for electricity. For the roof — the case where a person is hanging over an edge on a fall arrest system and the only other person on site has to get to them — nothing says the rescuer stays attached. There is no control requiring the second person to be on travel restraint or clipped to a rated anchor before approaching the casualty, the edge or the anchor line, and no instruction not to unclip to move faster. Running to the edge unattached to look over is precisely how the second person dies, and the step that names that hazard never addresses it. Second, steps[11].controls[6] allocates the emergency to three people: "One person makes the call, another runs the rescue, a third meets the ambulance at the gate." This statement crews every harness job and every roof trip for exactly two — whenRequired, steps[0].controls[2], steps[6].controls[2], steps[7].controls[7] and steps[11].controls[3] all say two. With the casualty down, one person is left to make the call, run the rescue and meet the ambulance. The emergency field's own shock paragraph gets this right ("There are two of you on this job for a reason"), and this control does not.
blocking.fix: Add an administrative control to steps[11] before the 000 item: the rescuer goes onto travel restraint or clips to a rated anchor before approaching the casualty, the edge, the anchor line or the fragile sheet, and does not unclip to move faster — a rescuer who goes over is two casualties and no rescue. Then rewrite steps[11].controls[6] for a crew of two: the survivor puts 000 on speaker and keeps working the rescue rather than stopping to make the call, tells the operator the address, the gate to use and that it is a fall from height with a person suspended, and asks the site contact or the fire watch — who this statement already puts on site whenever a system is impaired — to meet the ambulance. If a third person is genuinely required for the rescue as planned, that is a crewing decision and belongs in steps[0].controls[2] with the two-person rule, not an assumption made at the moment of the fall.

blocking.field: steps[10].hazards[4] and steps[10].controls ("Come down, restore the system and hand the area back")
blocking.problem: A named hazard half controlled. steps[10].hazards[4] reads "Ladder or machine left set up for someone else to climb". steps[10].controls[4] answers the machine — "lower the machine fully with the key out and the isolator off" — and no control in the step answers the ladder. Nothing says to take it down, lay it flat, chain it or put it back in the ute. A platform ladder left standing in an unlocked plant room, or an extension ladder left against a parapet or a booster wall overnight, is a fall for a cleaner, a contractor or a kid, and it is the one hazard on this list that hurts somebody who never read the SWMS.
blocking.fix: Extend steps[10].controls[4] or add an administrative control beside it: every ladder comes down, is closed and laid flat or racked in the ute before you leave, and no ladder is left standing or leaning on site — not overnight, not over lunch, not "we're coming back tomorrow". If a ladder genuinely has to stay on site, it is laid flat and secured where it cannot be stood up, and the building contact is told where it is.

blocking.field: steps[9].controls[0].level ("Control everything that can fall from where you are")
blocking.problem: A work rule levelled as elimination and thereby ranked above the physical control that enforces it. steps[9].controls[0] reads "Nobody works, walks or parks under the work. That is the whole point of the exclusion zone" and is levelled "eliminate". That is a prohibition — nothing physical stops anyone walking under the work because this line exists. The control that does the work is steps[9].controls[1], levelled "isolate": "Hard barriers, a closed and signed door, or a person stationed at each entry, for the whole time anything is above head height." The document levels the identical control correctly twice elsewhere — steps[1].controls[1] and steps[5].controls[0] are both "isolate" for the same substance — so this is an inconsistency within the statement as well as a mis-level, and it is the pattern the ordering rule exists to prevent: the rule ends up printed above the barrier.
blocking.fix: Change steps[9].controls[0].level to "administrative" and move it into the administrative block below controls[1] and the two engineering controls, keeping the s 54 and s 55(3)(a) citation with it — both are quoted correctly. The step then reads isolate, engineering, engineering, administrative, administrative, ppe, which still passes the ordering rule and puts the hard barrier where the crew reads it first. Alternatively fold the sentence into controls[1] so the barrier and the rule travel together.

blocking.problem: The list of what makes a WHSQ notification incomplete in the one direction that matters after the electrical work this statement now covers. The paragraph reads: "so is a dangerous incident under s 37 — which expressly includes the fall or release from a height of any plant, substance or thing, and the collapse, overturning, failure or malfunction of plant required to be authorised for use." Both are accurate (s 37(f) and s 37(g)). But s 37(e) of the Work Health and Safety Act 2011 (Qld) reads simply "electric shock", and s 35 makes a dangerous incident a notifiable incident, so an electric shock in a ceiling void is notifiable to Workplace Health and Safety Queensland under s 38 whether or not anyone is injured. The very next paragraph correctly sets up the second notification to the electrical safety regulator, and it correctly says it is "NOT A SUBSTITUTE FOR THE FIRST" — but the trigger for that first notification, as this paragraph lists it, does not include a shock. A shock where nobody sees a doctor is not a serious electrical incident under Electrical Safety Act 2002 (Qld) s 11(b) unless it was at high voltage, so on the document as written a low-voltage shock with no doctor visit gets notified to neither regulator, when it is squarely an s 37(e) dangerous incident.
blocking.fix: Add electric shock to the s 37 list in the NOTIFICATION paragraph: "s 37 expressly includes electric shock (s 37(e)), the fall or release from a height of any plant, substance or thing, and the collapse, overturning, failure or malfunction of plant required to be authorised for use." Then add to the run of examples: any shock a technician takes in a ceiling void or at a board is notified to WHSQ under s 37(e) even if he gets up and says he is fine, and separately to the electrical safety regulator if a doctor sees him or it was at high voltage.

blocking.field: ppe and emergency (no alarm or noise provision anywhere)
blocking.problem: A hazard of this specific trade that the document never names. The activity is AS 1851 routine service — detectors, sounders and strobes at ceiling level — and the words noise, hearing and evacuation appear nowhere in the statement. Two gaps follow. First, there is no hearing protection in an eleven-item ppe list, and no instruction about working beside or testing an alarm device at close range from a ladder platform or a basket; an alarm sounder going off unexpectedly a metre from your head while you are at the top of a platform ladder is a startle as much as a noise dose, and the startle is what takes you off the ladder. Second, there is no plan for the building's evacuation alarm activating while a technician is twelve metres up in a basket or standing on a roof. The emergency field covers fire while the system is impaired and tells the fire watch what to do on the ground, but says nothing to the person who is elevated — and the wrong instinctive response, hurrying the descent or climbing out, is the dangerous one.
blocking.fix: Add hearing protection to ppe for work at or near alarm devices. Add an administrative control to steps[3] and steps[5]: tell the panel operator and the crew before any test that can sound a device, and nobody is on a ladder or has hands off the basket controls when a sounder is initiated within reach. Add a short emergency paragraph, BUILDING ALARM OR EVACUATION WHILE YOU ARE UP: stop work, do not rush and do not climb out; lower the basket on the normal controls at normal speed, or walk the roof back to the hatch on the route you came by; the ground person confirms with the building contact whether it is your test or a real event before anyone moves off the assembly point, and if it is real the impairment and the fire watch position are reported to the brigade on arrival.
